Lake Victoria. Africa's largest lake by surface area, spanning approximately twenty-six thousand six hundred square miles across the borders of Tanzania, Uganda, and Kenya, Lake Victoria is the source of the White Nile and has been vital to the societies surrounding it for millennia, supporting fisheries, transportation, and agriculture.

Victoria is the world's second-largest freshwater lake by surface area after Lake Superior in North America, though shallower than most large lakes. It is bordered by three nations: Tanzania to the south and west, Uganda to the north, and Kenya to the east. The lake is fed by numerous rivers and seasonal rainfall, and the White Nile originates here, flowing northward through Sudan and Egypt.

British explorer John Hanning Speke named the lake Victoria in eighteen fifty-eight in honor of Queen Victoria. Over thirty million people depend on it for drinking water, fishing, and transportation. The introduction of the Nile perch in the nineteen-fifties led to the extinction of hundreds of endemic fish species, one of history's worst ecological disasters. The lake is divided among three nations by colonial boundaries, making water-sharing agreements critical for regional stability.
